sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 of the 1923 Clayton atlas shows the centre of the town on both sides of North Central Avenue, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 11 degrees on the page. It runs from the first blocks beyond Academy Avenue at the top to Centre Street at the bottom, with North Pearl Street along the west edge. Academy Avenue crosses the sheet diagonally and Church Alley, a 20 foot street, runs east from North Central Avenue through blocks 35 and 36. Most of the buildings are frame dwellings of one to two and a half storeys, drawn in yellow, with sheds and stables behind them. The principal buildings are the Clayton Hotel on the east side of North Central Avenue near Academy Avenue, a garage with concrete floor and capacity for six cars on the west side, Trinity M.E. Church with its Sabbath School, and Samuel S. Downs's sawing and planing mill with lumber storage on Church Alley, where fuel wood and coal are also kept and no watchman is employed. A brick hardware store with hollow tile construction stands at the corner of North Central Avenue and Church Alley. Water pipes of 6 and 8 inches are marked in the streets, with hydrants and dry hydrants at the corners. The east side of the sheet is largely open ground with scattered lots and farm buildings. A north arrow and compass rose are in the upper right, and the scale bar is at the foot of the sheet. Block numbers 27, 28, 34, 35 and 36 appear, with older numbers in parentheses.
notes: North Central Avenue is today North Delsea Drive; East and West Academy Avenue are East Academy Street and West Academy Street; East and West Centre are East Center Street and West Center Street.
The west half of Centre Street is lettered 'W. GENTRE' on this sheet, apparently a misprint or a damaged C for Centre.
East Church Alley is about 20 ft wide and was left out of the control points (under the detector's minimum width).
East Church Alley is hand-picked as control; the sheet is drawn slightly long north-south, so the alley sits about 9 m south of modern Church Lane and does not line up with sheet 9 at the east edge.

50 ft. N. Central Av (North Delsea Drive), Academy, Centre (W. Centre printed W. GENTRE); Clayton Hotel, Trinity M.E. Church, Downs sawing mill. One part. Drawn about 3 percent long north-south: E. Church Alley lands about 9 m south of modern Church Lane and steps 10-15 m against sheet 9 at the seam.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 of the 1923 Clayton atlas shows the commercial centre of the town astride North Central Avenue, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 12 degrees on the page. It extends from Centre Street at the top to West Clayton Avenue and the railroad at the bottom, and from North Pearl Street on the west to the open lots east of the avenue; Maple and High streets cross it. West of the avenue the blocks hold dwellings, a bakery with an oven and a feed store, a drug store, the public library, the B. Cohn and Co. shirt factory with light and power by electricity, a garage with capacity for twenty cars drawn in pink, and a restaurant. East of the avenue the post office, an auto repair shop, the Presbyterian Church, the Strand Theatre (movies) and the Clayton National Bank stand along the frontage, with hot houses on East High Street, while the ground behind is mostly open. Dwellings are frame and shown in yellow; lots are numbered with older numbers in parentheses, and blocks 43, 46, 47, 63 and 64 are lettered. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inches run in the cross streets with hydrants at the corners. The railroad (W. J. and S. R.R., P.R.R.) crosses the foot of the sheet. Part of North Pearl Street and the adjoining block of sheet 2 are lettered at the top left. A north arrow and compass rose are in the lower right.
notes: North Central Avenue (South Central Avenue south of Clayton) is today North and South Delsea Drive.
West and East Centre are West and East Center Street; West Maple is Maple Street.
The street names are lettered with alternates in parentheses, North Pearl (South Pearl) and North Central Av. (South Central Av.).
The railroad at the foot of the sheet is lettered W. J. and S. R.R. and P.R.R.
50 ft. Town centre on N. Central Av: Centre, Maple, High, Clayton; Strand Theatre, library, bank, P.R.R. One part.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 of the 1923 Clayton atlas covers the residential and civic blocks west of the town centre, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 11 degrees on the page so that North Broad Street runs nearly up the sheet. The sheet spans from West Centre Street at the top to West Clayton Avenue at the bottom, and from beyond North Broad Street on the west to North Pearl Street along the east edge, with West Maple and West High streets crossing between them. Blocks 32, 42, 43, 44, 45, 60 and 62 are shown. Nearly every building is a frame dwelling of one to two and a half storeys, drawn in yellow with small outbuildings, stables and sheds behind; lots are long and narrow and numbered with both current and older house numbers. The main civic building is the Town Hall and Opera House on the north side of West High Street at North Pearl Street, with the fire department station (a small brick building) and a hook and ladder truck house beside it. In the south-west block the H. Linsk and Co. dress factory is drawn, a frame building with power and lights by electricity. Four-inch water pipes are marked in West Centre, West Maple and West High streets and a six-inch pipe in North Pearl Street, with hydrants at the corners. A note at the west end of West Centre Street gives the distance to the first rail of the railroad, which lies on the neighbouring sheet 5. Street names are given with their alternative south names in parentheses, as in North Broad (South Broad) and North Pearl (South Pearl).
notes: West Centre is today West Center Street; West Maple is Maple Street.
Town Hall and Opera House, fire department and hook and ladder truck house on West High Street at North Pearl.
H. Linsk and Co. dress factory in the south-west block.
50 ft. West Centre to West Clayton Av, North Broad to North Pearl; Town Hall and Opera House. Pilot sheet; grid turned about 11 degrees. One part.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 of the 1923 Clayton atlas covers the railroad corridor on the west side of the town centre, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. The Pennsylvania Railroad line (marked P.R.R.) runs down the sheet a little east of its middle, with North Atlantic Avenue, a 60 ft street, beside it on the west. East of the tracks the west ends of West Centre, West Maple and West High streets stop at the railroad; west of it West Brookfield runs off diagonally to the north-west and West High continues on its own angle, with West Clayton Avenue along the bottom edge. Industry clusters near the tracks. At the top, north of West Centre, are the mills of the New Jersey Cotton Products Co. Inc. (cotton shoddy), with cement-floored manufacturing buildings, picker house, cotton warehouse, office, a loading platform along a siding and a steel water tower. On West Maple stands the Silver-Chamberlin Co. brush factory, a concrete-block manufacturing building with warehouse and coal house. West of North Atlantic Avenue is the Hungerford and Terry Inc. filter manufacturing plant with its machine shop. The passenger station, a brick building, stands east of the tracks between West Maple and West High, and a freight depot lies beside the line further north. The west half of the sheet is largely undeveloped: long narrow lots laid out on both sides of West High in block 59, with scattered dwellings, coops and sheds, and the large open block 41. Water pipes are marked in the east-west streets and in North Atlantic Avenue. The east edge meets sheet 4, which repeats the street ends but has almost no buildings in common.
notes: North Atlantic Avenue is today Atlantic Avenue; the railroad is the Vineland Secondary in OpenStreetMap.
West Centre, West Maple and West High end at the railroad right of way east of the tracks, where modern Thomas Street now runs; Thomas Street is not drawn.
New Jersey Cotton Products Co. Inc. (cotton shoddy), Hungerford and Terry Inc. filter manufacturing, Silver-Chamberlin Co. brush factory, passenger station and freight depot.

50 ft. Railroad corridor (P.R.R.) with North Atlantic Av (now Atlantic Avenue), West High, West Brookfield, West Clayton Av; NJ Cotton Products Co., Silver-Chamberlin brush factory, Hungerford & Terry filters, passenger station. Only three junctions (Atlantic/High, Atlantic/Clayton, rail/Clayton); weak, placed with help of the second pass. One part. Rotation pinned by a derived point (sheet 4 rotation).

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 of the 1923 Clayton atlas covers the north-west edge of the town, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 10 degrees on the page. It lies between North Broad Street on the west and North Pearl Street on the east, with West Academy Avenue crossing the top and West Centre Street closing the foot. The centre of the sheet is block 33, a large open tract with only a few dwellings on its edges, and west of North Broad Street block 32 holds a scatter of dwellings and outbuildings on long lots. Along West Academy Avenue a few frame houses, a pink-coloured building of larger size and several barns and sheds stand on the north side, and a small group of houses lies on the south side. Near the foot, dwellings and a stable stand on lots fronting West Centre Street and North Pearl Street. Water pipes of 4, 6 and 8 inches are marked in West Academy Avenue and West Centre Street, with dry hydrants at several corners. The upper left corner shows the end of North Union Street meeting West Academy Avenue, where the avenue bends. Block numbers 26, 27, 32 and 33 appear with older numbers in parentheses, and adjoining sheet numbers 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 and 13 are lettered at the margins. A north arrow and compass rose stand at the left, and the scale bar at the foot.
notes: West Academy Avenue is today West Academy Street; West Centre is West Center Street; North Union Street is the line of today's Aura Road.
50 ft. N. Broad to N. Pearl, W. Academy to W. Centre; mostly open block 33. One part; 4 points; seam correction held (8.6 m move from a 0.29 match contradicted its neighbours).

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7 of the 1923 Clayton atlas covers the north-west of the town around North Broad Street, between West North Street at the top and the blocks south of West Clinton Street, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 11 degrees on the page so that the streets run square to it. The west half is dominated by the works of F. M. Pierce and Co., a hollow ware glass factory marked as not in operation: a furnace house with its glass pots, batch, mould, clay and cleaning rooms, a box house, soda storage, several warehouses, hay sheds and a coal bin, served by a railroad siding of the P.R.R. (W.J. and S.S.R.R.) that runs in from the west across the factory lot. A note records a locomotive tire used as the fire alarm. North Broad Street runs down the middle of the sheet and is drawn with a jog west of the factory, its northern stretch lying further east than its southern one. East of Broad are residential blocks 21, 22 and 27 along West North, West Howard and West Clinton streets, built up with frame dwellings, stables and sheds on narrow lots, and divided north-south by a 23 ft street lettered Not Named. West of Broad and south of West Clinton, block 26 is laid out in lots with a few dwellings and coops, and North Union Street crosses the south-west corner, where sheet 13 adjoins. Water pipes of four and six inches are marked in West Howard and West Clinton streets.
notes: The 23 ft street lettered Not Named between West Howard and West Clinton is today Goodwin Lane.
North Broad north of the glass works is drawn about 25 m east of today's straight Broad Street line; junctions on that stretch were left out of the fit.
F. M. Pierce and Co. hollow ware glass factory, not in operation in 1923, with a railroad siding.

50 ft. North Broad between West North and south of West Clinton; F. M. Pierce & Co. hollow ware glass factory (not in operation). North Broad north of the glass works drawn about 25 m east of the modern line (left out). Not Named 23 ft street = Goodwin Lane. Three junctions; weak. One part. Goodwin / Clinton hand-picked (detector locked on a lot line); seam correction held.

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 of the 1923 Clayton atlas covers North Central Avenue north of the town centre, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 11 degrees on the page. The avenue runs from top to bottom along the sheet, with West North, West Howard and West Clinton streets entering from the west and a 23 foot street lettered Not Named running parallel to the avenue near the west edge. West of the avenue the blocks 20, 21 and 23 hold rows of frame dwellings on narrow lots, with hot houses, stables and sheds behind them and an auto repairing shop with a concrete floor and one gasoline tank near the avenue. East of the avenue the ground is mostly open, with a farm, barns and a store house, and in the upper right the W. Reed Skinner greenhouses with concrete block walls, labelled florist. A note at the top reads No Exposure. Water pipes of 4, 6 and 8 inches are marked in the streets and the avenue, with hydrants at the corners. Block 27 appears at the foot with block 28 on the east; neighbouring sheets 2, 6 and 7 are lettered at the margins. The north arrow and compass rose are at the right, and the scale bar at the foot.
notes: North Central Avenue is today North Delsea Drive; West North, West Howard and West Clinton are West North Street, West Howard Street and West Clinton Street.
The street lettered Not Named, 23 ft wide, is today Goodwin Lane.
W. Reed Skinner, florist: hot houses with concrete block walls.
50 ft. N. Central Av from W. North to W. Clinton; Goodwin Lane is the Not Named 23 ft street; Skinner greenhouses. One part.

sheet-9.description: Sheet 9 of the 1923 Clayton atlas covers the east side of the town centre, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 11 degrees on the page. North Main Street runs down the left of the sheet and North New Street down the right, with East Academy Avenue crossing the top diagonally, East Centre Street across the middle and East High Street at the foot. East Church Alley, a 20 foot street, enters from the west at upper left. Blocks 35, 36, 37, 47 and 48 are numbered, with older numbers in parentheses. The buildings are mostly frame dwellings of one to two and a half storeys with stables, coops and sheds; the one building of note is a synagogue, drawn in pink, with heat by hot air and lights by electricity, on East Centre Street. A wagon shed and a large barn stand in the block fronting East High Street. Much of the ground between the streets, and the large block between East Academy Avenue and East Centre Street, is open. A cemetery is lettered at the upper right beside the title oval and a small office building stands near it, with No Exposure notes along the east and north margins. Water pipes of 6 inches are marked in the streets, with dry hydrants at several corners. A north arrow and compass rose are at the right and the scale bar at the foot. Neighbouring sheets 2, 3, 10 and 11 are lettered at the margins.
notes: East Academy Avenue is today East Academy Street; East Centre is East Center Street; North Main and North New are North Main Street and North New Street.
East Church Alley is 20 ft wide and is today Church Lane; it was left out of the control points.
The fitted scale is about 7.67 px/ft against about 7.95 on the neighbouring 50 ft sheets, so the blocks between East Centre and East High are drawn about 4 percent shorter than the modern streets.
50 ft. N. Main to N. New, E. Academy to E. High; synagogue. Fits 7.68 px/ft (about 3.5 percent small, drawn short north-south). One part.

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 of the 1923 Clayton atlas covers the east side of the town at 100 feet to an inch, drawn with north straight up the page and the street grid turned about 6 degrees. It runs from East Academy Avenue at the top to East Chestnut at the bottom, and from North and South New streets on the west to North Turner Avenue on the east, with North and South Vine and North and South Green streets between them and East Centre, East High, East Clayton Avenue (South) and East Linden crossing. The north-west block 38 is a ball park with a grand stand. The large blocks 39, 50, 51, 52, 68 and 87 east of Vine and Green are mostly open land with only scattered dwellings, coops and sheds; block 51 between North Green and North Turner Avenue is empty apart from a few outbuildings. Housing is concentrated in the south-west, in blocks 49, 66, 67, 85, 86, 93 and 94 along North and South New, Vine and Green streets and on East High, East Clayton Avenue and East Linden: rows of one and two storey frame dwellings on narrow lots with coops and stables behind. A small ice cream factory stands in block 66 and a rug weaving shop near South Vine. Four- and six-inch water pipes with hydrants are marked in East Clayton Avenue, East Linden and South New. Margin notes on the west edge name East Clayton Avenue and East Linden Street where they continue onto sheets 9 and 11, and the top margin is marked no exposure.
notes: East Academy Avenue is today East Academy Street; East Centre is East Center Street; North Turner Avenue is Turner Street; East Clayton Avenue is also lettered (South).
The sheet fits with a second-order polynomial; a first-order fit leaves 4 to 6 m residuals along East Centre and East Academy, so the drawing is slightly distorted.
The line between North Green and North Turner Avenue in line with East High is a block boundary, not a street; East High Street / Turner Street was left out.
Ball park with grand stand in block 38; small ice cream factory in block 66.
100 ft. East side: East Academy to East Chestnut, New to North Turner Av; ball park. Turned about 6 degrees; second-order fit. One part.

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 of the 1923 Clayton atlas covers the south end of the town on both sides of South Central Avenue, drawn at 100 feet to an inch (the scale is lettered under the title oval) and turned about 11 degrees on the page. It runs from East High Street at the top to West Walnut Street at the foot, and from South Pearl Street and the railroad (W. J. and S. R.R., P.R.R.) on the west to South New Street on the east. West of the avenue the blocks between West Clayton Avenue and West Morton Avenue hold dwellings, a Baptist church, a tin shop, a milk depot and poultry houses, with block numbers 81, 82, 89, 90, 121, 122 and 148. East of the avenue, blocks 64, 65, 83, 84, 91 and 92 are laid out in narrow lots, largely vacant, with a junk store near East Clayton Avenue; the Clayton and Glassboro Water Co. pumping station stands on East Chestnut Street with its wells, a steel tower and a compound pump. Farther south the ground is open farmland: Fisler Farm, Grove Lawn with a long poultry house and corn cribs, A. Glerum's florist with hot houses on West Morton Avenue, and Hallock's Farm at the foot of the sheet. The north arrow and compass rose are at the top and the scale bar at the foot. Blocks of sheets 3, 4, 9, 10 and 12 are lettered at the margins.
notes: South Central Avenue is today South Delsea Drive; West Morton Avenue is Morton Street; West Walnut is Walnut Street.
East Clayton Avenue is lettered again beside North New Street at the right edge, where the road turns north-east.
Clayton and Glassboro Water Co. pumping station is lettered with its wells; the text on the notes beside it says water is pumped from wells to the tank and direct to the mains if necessary.
100 ft. S. Central Av south of Clayton: Linden, Chestnut, Morton, Walnut; water pumping station; farms. One part.

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 of the 1923 Clayton atlas covers the south-west of the town at 100 feet to an inch, from West Clayton Avenue at the top to West Erie and West League avenues at the bottom, and from South Roosevelt Boulevard on the west to the blocks beyond South Broad Street on the east. The railroad (W.J. and S.R.R., P.R.R.) runs down the sheet a little east of centre, with South Penn Street beside it on the west. Most of the sheet is a laid-out but almost empty grid: the long blocks 110 to 164 between South Roosevelt Boulevard and South Cedar, crossed by West Laver, West May, West Dorothy and West Poe avenues, West Lincoln Driveway and West Erie Avenue, carry no buildings at all, and notes along the west edge say vacant beyond. Building is concentrated along West Clayton Avenue at the top, where A. S. Clark and Co. has a flour and feed store with hay sheds and a coal shed, with a bakery and scattered dwellings and poultry houses behind. East of the tracks stands the Fisler and Crane lumber and mill work yard, with a lumber shed, store house, woodworking mill, cement block manufacturing shed and scattered small piles of lumber along a curving siding. Further east, blocks 81 and 89 between West Linden and West Chestnut hold frame dwellings on narrow lots, and a north-south street lettered West Linden, marked not open, borders the empty block 88. South of West Chestnut a row of poultry houses fills block 147, and South Broad Street runs diagonally down to West Morton Avenue and West Walnut, with a few dwellings and a hen house in block 165.
notes: South Cedar south of West Chestnut and most of the avenues east of South Roosevelt Boulevard were paper streets in 1923; today's streets there (Cedar Street, Jean Street, Novack Drive) follow other lines. Only the Roosevelt Boulevard junctions, Cedar Avenue north of Chestnut and South Broad Street were used as control.
West Morton Avenue is today Morton Street; West Walnut is Walnut Street; West Lincoln Driveway is Lincoln Drive; South Cedar north of West Chestnut is Cedar Avenue.
A. S. Clark and Co. flour and feed, Fisler and Crane lumber and mill work.
100 ft. South-west: West Clayton Av to West Erie/League, South Roosevelt Blvd to South Broad; mostly empty paper-street grid; A. S. Clark & Co., Fisler & Crane lumber. One part.

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13 of the 1923 Clayton atlas covers the north-western outskirts of the town at 100 feet to an inch, turned about 52 degrees on the page so that West Academy Avenue runs diagonally from upper left to lower right. It reaches from North Glassboro Road, which bounds the sheet on the north-west and north, to West Brookfield on the south-west, and from North Garden Avenue in the west to North Union Street along the east edge. West Carvin crosses the upper half parallel to West Academy Avenue, and the railroad (W.J. and S.R.R., P.R.R.) runs diagonally across the lower right with North Atlantic Avenue beside it on the west; North Atlantic, the railroad and North Union converge near the end of West Carvin. Most of the sheet is laid out in long narrow lots in blocks 17, 18, 24, 30 and 31 with only scattered frame dwellings, hen houses and sheds; much of it is empty. The Clayton Public School, a brick building heated by steam and lit by electricity, stands in block 25 between the railroad and North Union. At the bottom edge the north end of the New Jersey Cotton Products Co. works appears, continued on sheet 5. A short West Clinton Street enters from the east edge, an alley marked not open crosses the top right corner, and North Roosevelt Boulevard touches the bottom left corner beside block 29.
notes: North Union is today Aura Road; North Glassboro Road (west side) is Coyle Road; West Carvin is Carvin Street; North Garden Avenue is Garden Avenue.
Fitted scale is about 6 percent larger than 100 ft to an inch (4.23 px/ft against about 4.0 on sheet 12); the junctions are consistent at under 2.5 m, so the sheet appears drawn slightly off scale.
Atlantic Avenue / West Academy Street and the Aura Road rail crossing were left out of the fit (5 to 6 m residuals in the tangle where Atlantic, Union and the railroad meet).
Clayton Public School in block 25.

100 ft, turned about 52 degrees. North-west: North Glassboro Rd (Coyle Road), West Carvin, West Academy Av, North Garden Av, North Union (Aura Road); Clayton Public School. Fits about 6 percent larger than 100 ft. One part.
